---
title: "FALCONAge"
subtitle: "Biological age and aging-clock scoring from multiomic data, in Python and R."
body-classes: falcon-home
---

FALCONAge applies 68 published human aging clocks to DNA methylation, clinical chemistry and NMR
metabolomics data. Every clock ships its coefficients and runs offline. Each score is reported
with its unit, the source of its coefficients and its technical standard error.

The input is data that is already preprocessed and quality controlled: a beta matrix from an
array pipeline such as [methylarray](https://github.com/bhagesh-h/methylarray), a GEO series
matrix, a clinical chemistry table or a Nightingale NMR table.

## Run it in three commands

You need [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) and nothing else.
[Install](start/install.qmd) covers Docker itself and other ways to install.

**1. Get the image** (once, about 430 MB to download):

```bash
docker pull bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu
```

**2. See it work** on a small synthetic dataset, in about a minute:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu demo
```

**3. Run your own data.** Put your beta matrix and, if you have one, a sample sheet with each
sample's age, sex and tissue in the current folder:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu run betas.csv --samples samples.csv
```

Open `betas_falconage/report.html`. [Your first run](start/quickstart.qmd) explains every file the
run writes and how to read the report.

## Input

| Input | Reader | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Beta matrix (CSV, TSV, Parquet, `.h5ad`) | `read_betas()` | Normalised betas in either orientation; EPIC v2 identifiers are harmonised |
| GEO series matrix | `read_series_matrix()` | Sample characteristics become sample annotation |
| Targeted panel | `read_panel()` | Pyrosequencing, EpiTYPER, amplicon; the declared CpG list is checked, not intersected |
| ComputAgeBench study | `read_computage_bench()` | 65 harmonised case-control studies, pinned to a commit |
| Clinical chemistry | `read_clinical()` | Units declared per column, never inferred |
| Nightingale NMR | `read_nightingale()` | Column names translated to the names the scores were fitted with |

Raw IDATs, sequencing coverage files and proteomic or transcriptomic tables are not read.
Normalisation, detection filtering and sample QC are done upstream.

## Output

- One score per sample per clock, for every catalogued clock the input supports
- **A technical standard error on every score**, propagated from published per-probe
  reliability through each clock's weights, and a distribution-free prediction interval
- A coverage map of every clock's CpGs across the genome, a coverage table per clock, and the
  expected shift in years caused by missing probes
- A run manifest recording the package and registry versions, the SHA-256 of every coefficient
  file, the reliability table behind the intervals, the floating-point precision, the
  imputation policy and every warning raised

**Execution.** One numerical core in Python, called from R through reticulate, so a result is the same in either language.

**Refusals.** A saliva sample scored on a whole-blood clock (measured at 3.83–16.46 years of
error in the same people). Cell-free DNA on any array clock. Age acceleration on a pace-of-aging
clock. A cohort-centred clock given one sample. Each refusal names the measurement behind it.

In R, `citation("FALCONAge")`. The machine-readable version is
[CITATION.cff](https://github.com/bhagesh-h/FALCONAge/blob/main/CITATION.cff), which is what
GitHub's *Cite this repository* button reads.

The clock FALCONAge computed for you is somebody else's work, and citing
FALCONAge does not cite it. Every registry entry carries its primary
reference, so the list for an analysis comes out of the analysis:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python

```python
fa.registry.load().get("dnamphenoage").cite("bibtex")
```

### R

```r
cite_clock("dnamphenoage", "bibtex")
```

:::
